title: Rust
description: A complete, from-zero guide to the Rust programming language: installing the toolchain on Windows and Linux, syntax, ownership and memory, the standard library, Cargo, popular crates, and how to build and ship real programs.

Getting Started.What Is Rust:
Rust is a systems programming language focused on **safety, speed, and concurrency**. It was originally created at Mozilla and is now developed by the Rust Foundation and a large open-source community. It compiles to native machine code (no virtual machine, no garbage collector at runtime) and is used for everything from operating systems and browsers to command-line tools, web backends, and embedded devices. As of this guide, current stable Rust is in the **1.9x** series, and `cargo new` defaults new projects to the **2024 edition** (covered in [rustup, Toolchains and Editions](/rust/rustup-toolchains-editions/)) — but Rust ships new stable releases every six weeks with no major-version breaks, and the language fundamentals covered throughout this guide are stable, everyday Rust that hasn't changed in years and isn't expected to.

## Why people choose Rust

- **Memory safety without garbage collection.** Rust's compiler enforces rules at compile time (the "borrow checker") that eliminate whole classes of bugs — use-after-free, double-free, null pointer dereferences, data races — without needing a garbage collector to clean things up at runtime.
- **Performance close to C/C++.** Because there's no GC pause and the compiler produces highly optimized native code, Rust programs are typically as fast as equivalent C or C++ programs.
- **Fearless concurrency.** The same ownership rules that make Rust memory-safe also catch most data races at compile time, so writing correct multi-threaded code is much harder to get wrong.
- **A modern toolchain.** Cargo (Rust's build tool and package manager), rustfmt (formatter), and clippy (linter) are official, first-class tools included from day one — not bolted-on third-party add-ons.
- **Great error messages.** The compiler is famous for explaining *why* code doesn't compile and often suggesting the fix directly.

## What Rust is *not* good at (tradeoffs)

- **Learning curve.** Ownership and borrowing are concepts most languages don't have, so there's real upfront learning — this guide spends an entire section on it.
- **Compile times.** Rust does a lot of work at compile time to guarantee safety, so builds — especially clean release builds of large projects — can be slower than dynamic languages or Go.
- **Verbosity for quick scripts.** For a 10-line throwaway script, a dynamic language like Python or Lua will usually get you there faster. Rust shines as projects grow.

## What you can build with Rust

- **CLI tools** — `ripgrep`, `fd`, `bat`, `exa` are popular Rust CLI tools that replaced classic Unix utilities for many developers.
- **Web backends** — frameworks like Axum, Actix Web, and Rocket.
- **Systems software** — parts of Firefox, the Linux kernel (experimental), Discord's backend infrastructure, and Dropbox's file sync engine are written in Rust.
- **Embedded and WebAssembly** — Rust has first-class support for `no_std` embedded targets and compiles cleanly to WebAssembly.
- **Game engines and tools** — Bevy is a popular Rust game engine.

## How this guide is organized

This guide assumes **zero prior Rust knowledge**, but does assume you've programmed before in *some* language. It goes in this order:

1. **Getting Started** (this section) — installing Rust and running your first program.
2. **Syntax Basics** — variables, types, operators.
3. **Ownership and Memory** — the concept that makes Rust unique.
4. **Control Flow and Functions**, **Structs/Enums/Pattern Matching**, **Error Handling** — the everyday building blocks.
5. **Modules and Crates**, **Generics and Traits** — organizing and abstracting larger programs.
6. **Collections**, **Strings**, **I/O**, **Concurrency**, **Testing** — the standard library in depth.
7. **Cargo and Toolchain**, **Popular Crates**, **Building and Shipping** — the practical, "how do real projects work" material.
8. **Project** — a full worked example tying everything together.

Getting Started.Installing Rust on Linux:
The standard, recommended way to install Rust on any platform — including every Linux distribution, such as Arch Linux — is **rustup**, the official Rust toolchain installer. Avoid installing Rust from your distro's package manager (e.g. `pacman -S rust`) as your primary install: it works, but it makes upgrading, switching toolchains, and adding targets much harder than rustup does. Use rustup.

## Install with rustup (recommended)

Open a terminal and run:

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```

This downloads and runs the official rustup install script. It will:

1. Detect your platform.
2. Ask you to choose an installation option — press **Enter** to accept the default (`1) Proceed with installation (default)`), which installs the `stable` toolchain.
3. Add `~/.cargo/bin` to your `PATH` by editing your shell profile (e.g. `~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, or `~/.profile`).

After it finishes, either restart your terminal or run:

```bash
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
```

Then verify the install:

```bash
rustc --version
cargo --version
```

You should see version numbers like `rustc 1.9x.0 (...)` and `cargo 1.9x.0 (...)` — the exact patch number will depend on when you install, since Rust ships a new stable release every six weeks.

## Arch Linux specifics

Arch Linux has a `rust` package in the official repos, and it is kept reasonably up to date, but it still has the downsides above (no easy multi-toolchain support, no `rustup target add` for cross-compiling, no `rustup component add` for clippy/rustfmt on old toolchains). If you already have it installed via pacman and want to switch to rustup:

```bash
sudo pacman -Rns rust
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```

If you prefer pacman anyway (e.g. for a minimal container image), it works fine for simple use:

```bash
sudo pacman -S rust
```

but you won't get `rustup target add`, `rustup component add`, or easy `stable`/`beta`/`nightly` switching — you'll need `rustup` alongside it for that.

## What rustup actually installs

- **rustc** — the compiler.
- **cargo** — the build tool and package manager (covered in depth in the [Cargo and Toolchain](/rust/cargo-toml-explained/) section).
- **rustup** itself — a version manager for the other two, similar in spirit to `nvm` for Node.js or `pyenv` for Python.
- Standard library source and docs, so `rustup doc` opens local documentation without internet access.

## Uninstalling

```bash
rustup self uninstall
```

Getting Started.Installing Rust on Windows:
On Windows, Rust also uses **rustup**, but Windows needs one extra piece first: a linker and Windows API libraries, which come from Microsoft's build tools.

## Step 1: Install the Visual Studio Build Tools

Rust on Windows needs the MSVC linker (`link.exe`) unless you use the alternate GNU toolchain (covered below). Download and run the **Visual Studio Build Tools** installer from Microsoft:

1. Go to `visualstudio.microsoft.com/downloads/` and download **"Build Tools for Visual Studio"**.
2. Run the installer and select the **"Desktop development with C++"** workload.
3. Install (this downloads a few GB — it includes the MSVC compiler and Windows SDK).

This is a one-time setup step. You do **not** need the full Visual Studio IDE, just the Build Tools.

## Step 2: Install rustup

Go to `rustup.rs` and download `rustup-init.exe`, then run it. A console window opens showing installation options — press **Enter** to accept the default, which installs the `stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` toolchain and detects your Build Tools automatically.

Alternatively, from PowerShell:

```powershell
winget install Rustlang.Rustup
```

## Step 3: Verify

Open a new PowerShell or Command Prompt window (important: a *new* window, so `PATH` changes take effect) and run:

```powershell
rustc --version
cargo --version
```

## Avoiding the C++ Build Tools: the GNU toolchain

If you don't want to install Visual Studio Build Tools, you can use the GNU toolchain instead, which links against MinGW-w64 rather than MSVC:

```powershell
rustup toolchain install stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
rustup default stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
```

You'll still need a MinGW-w64 `gcc`/linker on your `PATH` (e.g. via MSYS2). For beginners, the MSVC route with Build Tools is the more common and better-supported path, and is what most tutorials assume.

## WSL as an alternative

Many Windows developers prefer running Rust inside **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**, which lets you follow the Linux install instructions exactly and avoids MSVC entirely. To set up WSL:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

Then inside the resulting Ubuntu shell, follow the [Installing Rust on Linux](/rust/installing-rust-on-linux/) page. This guide's Linux and Windows instructions both work fine — pick native Windows if you want to ship `.exe` files directly, or WSL if you're more comfortable in a Linux-like environment.

Getting Started.Your Editor Setup:
You can write Rust in any text editor, but a proper setup with autocompletion, inline errors, and go-to-definition will make learning dramatically faster since the compiler's feedback becomes immediate instead of appearing only when you run `cargo build`.

## VS Code + rust-analyzer (most common choice)

1. Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/).
2. Open the Extensions panel (`Ctrl+Shift+X`) and install **rust-analyzer** (the official language server extension, published by "The Rust Programming Language" team — not the older, now-deprecated "Rust" extension).
3. Open any folder containing a `Cargo.toml` file and rust-analyzer activates automatically. You'll get: inline type hints, autocompletion, jump-to-definition, inline error squiggles as you type, and a "Run" / "Debug" link above every `fn main()` and `#[test]`.

Recommended companion extensions:
- **CodeLLDB** — enables breakpoint debugging.
- **Even Better TOML** — syntax highlighting for `Cargo.toml`.

## Other editors

- **Neovim / Vim** — install `rust-analyzer` as a language server via `nvim-lspconfig` (Neovim) or a plugin manager. On Arch Linux, `rust-analyzer` is also available as a pacman package: `sudo pacman -S rust-analyzer`.
- **JetBrains RustRover** — a dedicated Rust IDE from JetBrains with built-in tooling, no extension needed.
- **Helix** — has rust-analyzer support built in with zero configuration once `rust-analyzer` is on your `PATH`.
- **Zed** — has native, fast rust-analyzer integration.

## Installing rust-analyzer as a standalone binary

If your editor needs the `rust-analyzer` binary directly rather than through an extension marketplace:

```bash
rustup component add rust-analyzer
```

This installs it alongside your toolchain, and most editor plugins can find it automatically once installed this way.

## Formatting on save

Once `rustfmt` is available (installed by default with rustup), most editors can be configured to format Rust files automatically on save. In VS Code with rust-analyzer, this is a built-in setting: search settings for "format on save" and enable it — rust-analyzer will use `rustfmt` automatically. Formatting conventions are covered in [clippy and rustfmt](/rust/clippy-and-rustfmt/).

Getting Started.Hello World:
Let's write and run your first Rust program two ways: directly with `rustc`, and then the way you'll actually work day-to-day, with Cargo.

## The plain rustc way

Create a file called `main.rs`:

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```

A few things to notice immediately:

- `fn main()` defines a function named `main` — the entry point every Rust *binary* program must have.
- `println!` looks like a function call but ends in `!` — that means it's a **macro**, not a function. Macros are code that generates code; `println!` expands into the actual formatting and printing logic at compile time. You'll use macros often (`println!`, `vec!`, `format!`) without needing to write your own for a long time.
- The line ends with a semicolon `;`, same as in C, Java, or JavaScript.

Compile and run it:

```bash
rustc main.rs
./main        # on Linux/macOS
main.exe      # on Windows (or just: .\main.exe in PowerShell)
```

`rustc` compiles `main.rs` directly into a native executable called `main` (or `main.exe` on Windows) in the current directory. This is fine for a single file, but real projects use Cargo instead — it handles compiling, dependencies, and more with one command.

## The Cargo way (what you'll actually use)

```bash
cargo new hello_world
cd hello_world
```

This creates:

```
hello_world/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    └── main.rs
```

`Cargo.toml` is the project's manifest (name, version, dependencies — covered fully in [Cargo.toml Explained](/rust/cargo-toml-explained/)). `src/main.rs` already contains the same "Hello, world!" program you just wrote by hand. Run it with:

```bash
cargo run
```

Cargo compiles the project (into a `target/` directory) and runs the resulting binary in one step. You'll see output like:

```
   Compiling hello_world v0.1.0 (/path/to/hello_world)
    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.42s
     Running `target/debug/hello_world`
Hello, world!
```

From here on, this entire guide assumes you're using `cargo new` and `cargo run` for every example — that's the normal, idiomatic way to work with Rust, even for tiny programs.

Getting Started.Cargo Quick Tour:
Cargo is Rust's build tool *and* package manager, combined into one program — similar in spirit to `npm` for JavaScript or `pip` + a build system for Python, but built in from day one and used by essentially every Rust project. This page is a fast tour; the full reference lives in [Cargo and Toolchain](/rust/cargo-toml-explained/).

## The commands you'll use constantly

```bash
cargo new my_project     # create a new binary project
cargo new my_lib --lib   # create a new library project (no main.rs, just lib.rs)
cargo build              # compile (debug mode, unoptimized, fast to compile)
cargo build --release    # compile with full optimizations (slower to compile, faster to run)
cargo run                # build (if needed) and run
cargo check              # type-check without producing a binary (much faster than build)
cargo test               # run all tests
cargo doc --open         # build and open documentation for your project + dependencies
```

`cargo check` is worth calling out specifically: while you're writing code, run `cargo check` instead of `cargo build` — it does everything except the final code generation step, so it's much faster and is exactly what you want for "does this compile?" feedback loops.

## Project layout Cargo expects

```
my_project/
├── Cargo.toml       # manifest: name, version, dependencies
├── Cargo.lock       # exact locked dependency versions (auto-generated, commit this for binaries)
├── src/
│   └── main.rs      # entry point for a binary
├── tests/           # integration tests (optional, covered in Testing section)
└── target/          # build output (auto-generated, do NOT commit this)
```

## Adding a dependency

```bash
cargo add rand
```

This fetches the latest compatible version of the `rand` crate from **crates.io** (the central Rust package registry, equivalent to npm's registry or PyPI) and adds it to `Cargo.toml` automatically. You can also edit `Cargo.toml` by hand:

```toml
[dependencies]
rand = "0.8"
```

Then run `cargo build` — Cargo downloads, compiles, and links the dependency (and its own dependencies, transitively) automatically. This whole workflow is explored in depth later in [Dependencies and Semantic Versioning](/rust/dependencies-and-semantic-versioning/) and [Popular Crates](/rust/serde-serialization/).

## `.gitignore`

`cargo new` automatically creates a `.gitignore` containing:

```
/target
```

`target/` can be multiple gigabytes for a large project with many dependencies — never commit it. `Cargo.lock` *should* be committed for binary projects (to guarantee reproducible builds) but is often left uncommitted for libraries (so downstream users resolve their own compatible versions) — this distinction is explained in [Dependencies and Semantic Versioning](/rust/dependencies-and-semantic-versioning/).

Getting Started.The Rust Toolchain Explained:
It's worth understanding, early on, what the pieces of "Rust" you just installed actually are and how they relate — this avoids confusion later when tutorials mention `rustup`, `rustc`, `cargo`, "nightly," or "editions" interchangeably.

## The three programs

- **rustc** — the actual compiler. Takes `.rs` source files and produces machine code. You'll rarely invoke `rustc` directly once you're using Cargo, since Cargo calls it for you with the right flags.
- **cargo** — the build tool / package manager / task runner. This is your daily interface: `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`, `cargo add`.
- **rustup** — the toolchain *manager*. It doesn't compile anything itself; it manages which version(s) of rustc/cargo are installed and active.

## Toolchains: stable, beta, nightly

Rust ships new stable releases every **six weeks**. At any time there are three "channels":

- **stable** — what you should use for almost everything. This is the default rustup installs.
- **beta** — the next stable release, being tested. Rarely used directly by application developers.
- **nightly** — built daily from the latest source, includes experimental/unstable features gated behind `#![feature(...)]` flags. Some tools (certain formatters, some crates, `cargo fmt -- --check` edge cases) or unstable language features require nightly. You'll occasionally see a `README` say "requires nightly" — that's what this means.

Switch or install channels with rustup:

```bash
rustup toolchain install nightly
rustup default nightly        # switch globally
rustup default stable         # switch back
rustup run nightly cargo build   # run one command on nightly without switching globally
```

A project can also pin its toolchain by adding a `rust-toolchain.toml` file to its root, which rustup reads automatically.

## Editions: 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024

Separately from stable/beta/nightly, Rust has **editions** — opt-in sets of syntax changes that avoid breaking old code. An edition is declared in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
edition = "2024"
```

Editions are *not* versions of the language in the semver sense — all editions are supported by the same compiler, and crates using different editions can even depend on each other. Editions exist so Rust can make small, deliberate breaking changes to syntax (e.g. how closures capture variables) without breaking the entire ecosystem at once. `cargo new` always picks the latest stable edition for you, so as a beginner you generally never need to think about this — just know what the field in `Cargo.toml` means when you see it.

## Components

`rustup component add <name>` installs extra pieces on top of a toolchain:

```bash
rustup component add clippy      # the linter
rustup component add rustfmt     # the formatter
rustup component add rust-src    # standard library source, needed by some tools
rustup component add rust-analyzer  # the language server
```

These are all installed by default with a standard `rustup-init` install, so you usually won't need to run these commands — but it's useful to know they exist if a specific component is ever missing (rustup will tell you exactly which command to run when this happens).

Syntax Basics.Constants and Statics:
Rust has two more ways to declare unchanging values beyond immutable `let` bindings: `const` and `static`.

## const

```rust
const MAX_PLAYERS: u32 = 4;
const PI: f64 = 3.14159265358979;
```

Key differences from `let`:

- **Type annotation is required** — `const` never infers.
- Can be declared in **any scope**, including outside any function (global to the whole module).
- The value **must be known at compile time** — you can't do `const X: i32 = some_function_call();` unless that function is itself a `const fn`.
- By convention, always `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`.
- A `const` isn't really a "variable" at all — every place it's used, the compiler substitutes the literal value directly (similar to `#define` in C, but type-checked).

```rust
const SECONDS_PER_HOUR: u32 = 60 * 60;

fn main() {
    println!("{}", SECONDS_PER_HOUR);
}
```

## static

```rust
static GREETING: &str = "Hello!";
```

`static` is similar to `const` but represents an actual fixed memory location that exists for the entire duration of the program (a "global"), rather than being inlined everywhere it's used. Mutable statics (`static mut`) exist but require `unsafe` to access, because mutable global state shared across threads is exactly the kind of thing Rust's safety guarantees are designed to prevent — you'll rarely need `static mut` as a beginner, and when you do want shared mutable global state, the idiomatic tools are things like `Mutex` (covered in [Shared State With Mutex and Arc](/rust/shared-state-with-mutex-and-arc/)) or the `OnceLock`/`LazyLock` types from the standard library.

## const vs static vs let: when to use which

| | Scope | Compile-time constant? | Mutable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `let` | local, inside a function/block | no, can be runtime value | with `mut` |
| `const` | anywhere, inlined at use sites | yes, always | never |
| `static` | anywhere, one fixed memory address | yes, always | only `unsafe` |

As a rule of thumb: use `let` (and `let mut`) for almost everything inside functions. Reach for `const` when you have a fixed value used in multiple places (magic numbers, config limits). You'll rarely need `static` directly as a beginner.

Syntax Basics.Scalar Types:
Rust is **statically typed**: every value has a known type at compile time. This page covers the scalar (single-value) types. Compound types (tuples, arrays) are covered here too; collections like `Vec` and `HashMap` get their own deep dive later.

## Integers

| Type | Size | Range (signed) or note |
|---|---|---|
| `i8` / `u8` | 8-bit | -128 to 127 / 0 to 255 |
| `i16` / `u16` | 16-bit | |
| `i32` / `u32` | 32-bit | **`i32` is the default integer type** |
| `i64` / `u64` | 64-bit | |
| `i128` / `u128` | 128-bit | |
| `isize` / `usize` | pointer-sized | matches the CPU architecture (64-bit on modern machines); used for indexing collections |

The `i` prefix means signed (can be negative), `u` means unsigned (zero or positive only). If you don't specify, integer literals default to `i32`, which is fast on essentially all modern hardware and big enough for most everyday values.

```rust
let a: i32 = -5;
let b: u8 = 255;
let c = 42; // inferred i32
```

Integer literals can use suffixes and separators for readability:

```rust
let million = 1_000_000; // underscores are just visual separators, ignored by the compiler
let byte = 255u8;         // type suffix directly on the literal
let hex = 0xff;
let octal = 0o77;
let binary = 0b1010;
```

**Overflow**: in debug builds, integer overflow (e.g. adding 1 to `u8::MAX`, which is 255) causes a **panic** (the program crashes with an error). In release builds, it wraps around silently by default (255 + 1 becomes 0) for performance reasons. If you need explicit control, the standard library provides `wrapping_add`, `checked_add`, `saturating_add`, and `overflowing_add` methods on every integer type.

## Floating point

```rust
let x = 2.0;      // f64 (default, double precision)
let y: f32 = 3.0; // f32 (single precision)
```

Rust follows IEEE-754 for floats, same as almost every modern language.

## Booleans

```rust
let is_active: bool = true;
let is_done = false;
```

One `bool`, one byte, `true` or `false` — no truthy/falsy conversion of other types happens automatically like in Python or JavaScript. An `if` condition in Rust *must* be an actual `bool`.

## Characters

```rust
let c: char = 'z';
let heart_eyed_cat = '😻';
```

Rust's `char` is a 4-byte **Unicode scalar value**, not a single byte like `char` in C. This means a Rust `char` can represent any Unicode code point directly, including emoji. Note the single quotes for `char` vs double quotes for string literals (`&str`) — this distinction matters and the compiler enforces it.

## Tuples

Group several values of *different* types into one compound value:

```rust
let person: (&str, i32, bool) = ("Alice", 30, true);

let (name, age, active) = person; // destructuring
println!("{name} is {age}");

println!("{}", person.0); // access by index too
```

The **unit type** `()` — an empty tuple — is the type of expressions that don't return a meaningful value, like `println!(...)`. You'll see `()` frequently as a function's implicit return type.

## Arrays

Fixed-size, same-type collections, stored on the stack:

```rust
let numbers: [i32; 5] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let zeros = [0; 10]; // shorthand: [value; count] -> ten zeros

println!("{}", numbers[0]);   // 1
println!("{}", numbers.len()); // 5
```

Arrays have a fixed length baked into their type (`[i32; 5]` is a different type from `[i32; 6]`). For a growable, heap-allocated list, you want `Vec<T>` instead — covered in [Vectors](/rust/vectors/).

Syntax Basics.Operators:
## Arithmetic

```rust
let sum = 5 + 3;
let diff = 5 - 3;
let product = 5 * 3;
let quotient = 5 / 3;   // integer division: 1 (truncates, doesn't round)
let remainder = 5 % 3;  // 2

let float_quotient = 5.0 / 3.0; // 1.6666... — normal float division
```

Integer division truncates toward zero — `5 / 3` is `1`, and `-5 / 3` is `-1`, not `-2`.

## Comparison

```rust
5 == 3   // false
5 != 3   // true
5 > 3    // true
5 < 3    // false
5 >= 5   // true
5 <= 4   // false
```

These all produce a `bool`.

## Logical

```rust
true && false   // AND, short-circuits
true || false   // OR, short-circuits
!true           // NOT -> false
```

Rust requires actual `bool` operands here — there's no automatic conversion from integers or other types the way C treats `0` as false.

## Compound assignment

```rust
let mut x = 5;
x += 1;  // x = 6
x -= 2;  // x = 4
x *= 3;  // x = 12
x /= 4;  // x = 3
x %= 2;  // x = 1
```

Note: Rust does **not** have `++` or `--` increment/decrement operators, unlike C, Java, or JavaScript. Use `x += 1` instead.

## Bitwise

```rust
let a = 0b1010;
let b = 0b0110;

a & b   // AND
a | b   // OR
a ^ b   // XOR
!a      // NOT
a << 1  // left shift
a >> 1  // right shift
```

## Range operators

```rust
0..5    // exclusive range: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
0..=5   // inclusive range: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

Ranges show up constantly in `for` loops and slicing — covered in [Loops](/rust/loops-loop-while-for/) and [Slices](/rust/slices/).

Syntax Basics.Shadowing:
**Shadowing** means declaring a new variable with the same name as a previous one using `let` again. It's different from mutation, and different from reassignment — it's genuinely a *new* variable that happens to reuse the old name.

```rust
fn main() {
    let x = 5;
    let x = x + 1;   // new variable, shadows the old x
    let x = x * 2;   // new variable again

    println!("{x}"); // 12
}
```

## Why this is useful (and not just confusing)

The clearest benefit: shadowing lets you **change a value's type** while reusing a meaningful name, which mutation (`mut`) can never do — a `mut` variable's type is fixed forever.

```rust
let spaces = "   ";          // spaces: &str
let spaces = spaces.len();   // spaces: usize — totally different type, same name

// vs. with mut, this is a compile error:
let mut spaces = "   ";
spaces = spaces.len(); // ERROR: expected `&str`, found `usize`
```

This pattern is genuinely common in real Rust code — parsing a string into a number and reusing the same conceptual name is a classic case:

```rust
let guess = "42";
let guess: u32 = guess.trim().parse().expect("not a number");
```

## Shadowing is scoped

Shadowing inside a block only lasts for that block; the outer variable reappears afterward:

```rust
fn main() {
    let x = 5;

    {
        let x = x * 2; // shadows only inside this block
        println!("inner x: {x}"); // 10
    }

    println!("outer x: {x}"); // 5, unaffected
}
```

## Shadowing vs mut: which to use

| | Can change type? | Creates new variable? | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `let mut x = ...; x = ...;` | No | No | A value that's genuinely updated in a loop/algorithm (a counter, an accumulator) |
| `let x = ...; let x = ...;` | Yes | Yes | Transforming a value through a pipeline of steps, reusing a clear name |

As a rule of thumb: reach for `mut` when a value is being updated repeatedly (like a loop counter), and reach for shadowing when you're transforming a value once or twice into its "final form" and don't need the intermediate versions afterward.

Ownership and Memory.Why Ownership Exists:
This is the single most important concept in Rust, and the thing that makes it genuinely different from almost every other mainstream language. Take your time with this section — everything else in Rust builds on it.

## The problem Rust is solving

Every program needs to manage memory. There are traditionally two approaches:

1. **Manual management (C, C++)** — you explicitly `malloc`/`free` (or `new`/`delete`). Fast, but easy to get wrong: forget to free memory (a **leak**), free it twice (**double-free**), or use it after freeing it (**use-after-free**). These bugs cause crashes and are historically the source of a huge fraction of security vulnerabilities in software.
2. **Garbage collection (Java, Python, Go, JavaScript, Lua)** — a background process automatically tracks which memory is still reachable and frees the rest. Safe and easy, but costs performance: GC pauses, memory overhead for tracking, and less predictable timing.

Rust takes a third path: **ownership**. The compiler tracks, at compile time, exactly when each piece of memory is no longer needed, and inserts the cleanup code automatically — with **zero runtime cost**, because all the checking happens before your program ever runs. If your code would have a memory bug, it simply won't compile. You fix it once, at compile time, instead of debugging it in production.

## The three rules of ownership

Rust's entire memory model boils down to three rules:

1. **Each value in Rust has a single owner** — one variable that's responsible for it.
2. **There can only be one owner at a time.**
3. **When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped** (its memory is freed automatically).

That's genuinely the whole idea. The next few pages work through exactly what "owner," "move," and "drop" mean in practice, with real code, because the rules above are easy to state and take some practice to feel natural.

## Stack vs heap, briefly

Ownership matters most for **heap-allocated** data — data whose size isn't known at compile time, or that needs to outlive the function that created it (like a growable `String` or `Vec`). Simple fixed-size values like integers live on the **stack** and are so cheap to copy that ownership rules barely matter for them in practice (this is the `Copy` trait, covered two pages from now). Understanding stack vs heap isn't strictly required to use Rust, but it explains *why* the rules exist:

- **Stack**: fast, fixed-size, automatically cleaned up when a function returns. Think of it as a stack of plates — last in, first out.
- **Heap**: for data whose size can grow or isn't known upfront (like a `String` you're building up, or a `Vec` you're pushing items into). Allocating heap memory takes a bit of bookkeeping, and — in a language without ownership rules or a GC — *someone* has to remember to free it later. Ownership is Rust's answer to "who does that bookkeeping, and when."

Ownership and Memory.Clone and Copy:
The previous page showed that integers copy automatically while `String`s move. This page explains the mechanism (`Copy` and `Clone`, two related but distinct traits) and how to explicitly duplicate a heap value when you actually want two independent copies.

## Clone: explicit, possibly expensive duplication

If you genuinely want a second, fully independent copy of heap data — including the heap allocation itself, not just the pointer — call `.clone()`:

```rust
let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1.clone(); // deep copy: new heap allocation, new data

println!("{s1} {s2}"); // both valid — this compiles fine
```

`.clone()` is always an explicit method call — Rust never clones implicitly behind your back, because cloning can be expensive (it might copy megabytes of data), and the language's philosophy is that costs should be visible in the code. When you see `.clone()` in Rust code, that's a deliberate signal: "yes, I want a real, independent copy here."

## Copy: implicit, cheap duplication

Some types are small enough and simple enough (no heap data, no destructor logic needed) that Rust allows them to be duplicated automatically on assignment, with no explicit `.clone()` needed. This is controlled by the `Copy` trait. Types that implement `Copy`:

- All the integer types (`i32`, `u8`, `usize`, etc.)
- `f32`, `f64`
- `bool`
- `char`
- Tuples, but *only* if every element inside is also `Copy` — `(i32, i32)` is `Copy`, but `(i32, String)` is not.

```rust
let x = 5;      // i32 is Copy
let y = x;      // copies, doesn't move
println!("{x}"); // fine, x is still valid
```

`String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, and most other heap-owning types deliberately do **not** implement `Copy` — because silently duplicating an entire heap allocation on every assignment would be a hidden performance cost, which goes against Rust's philosophy of making costs explicit.

## Making your own types Copy or Clone

For your own `struct`s and `enum`s, you can opt in with a derive attribute:

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

// or, if every field is itself Copy:
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Point2 {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

`#[derive(...)]` is covered fully in [Common Derivable Traits](/rust/common-derivable-traits/) — it automatically generates the trait implementation for you rather than requiring you to write it by hand. A type can only derive `Copy` if all of its fields are themselves `Copy` — the compiler checks and enforces this.

## Quick decision guide

- Need a real, independent second copy of heap data (a `String`, `Vec`, etc.)? Call `.clone()`.
- Working with small stack-only data (numbers, booleans, simple structs of numbers)? It's probably already `Copy` — nothing to do, it just works.
- Writing your own small, simple struct and want it to behave like a number (copy freely)? Add `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]`.

Error Handling.Panic and Unrecoverable Errors:
Rust splits errors into two categories: **unrecoverable** (things so wrong the program can't reasonably continue — handled by `panic!`, this page) and **recoverable** (expected failures a caller should handle — the `Result` type, next page). This page covers panics.

## What causes a panic

```rust
fn main() {
    panic!("something went horribly wrong");
}
```

Running this prints an error message, a note about setting `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` for a full stack trace, and exits with a non-zero status code. Panics also happen implicitly, from operations that have no sensible way to continue:

```rust
let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
v[99]; // panics: index out of bounds

let x: Option<i32> = None;
x.unwrap(); // panics: called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value

let x = 10 / 0; // in debug builds: panics with "attempt to divide by zero"
```

## Unwinding vs aborting

By default, a panic **unwinds** — Rust walks back up the stack, cleaning up (dropping) each value it passed through, then exits. You can configure a panic to **abort** immediately instead (skipping cleanup, exiting faster, and producing a smaller binary) by adding this to `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[profile.release]
panic = "abort"
```

This is a common choice for release binaries where you don't need to catch panics and want the smallest, fastest binary possible.

## When to actually use panic! yourself

As a rule of thumb: reach for `panic!` (or `.unwrap()`/`.expect()`, which panic internally) when:

- You're writing a **quick example, prototype, or test**, where crashing loudly on unexpected input is more helpful than silently continuing.
- The failure represents a genuine **bug** in your program's logic — a state that should be *impossible* if your code is correct (e.g. an array index you calculated yourself, that you've mathematically proven is always in bounds).
- You're **prototyping** and haven't decided on proper error handling yet — `.unwrap()` is a fine placeholder to come back to later.

For anything else — a file that might not exist, user input that might be malformed, a network request that might fail — use `Result` instead (next page), because these are *expected*, recoverable failure modes that a caller should be able to handle gracefully rather than having the whole program crash.

## .expect() over .unwrap() when you do panic intentionally

```rust
let f = std::fs::File::open("config.txt")
    .expect("config.txt should exist in the project root");
```

`.expect("message")` panics with your custom message if the value is `None`/`Err`, which is far more useful for debugging than `.unwrap()`'s generic message — prefer `.expect()` with a clear message whenever you do decide unwrapping is the right call.

Next: [Result and Recoverable Errors](/rust/result-and-recoverable-errors/).
Error Handling.Error Handling Crates:
The standard library gives you everything *needed* for error handling (`Result`, `?`, `std::error::Error`), but two community crates are so widely used that they're considered close to a de facto standard: **thiserror** for libraries, and **anyhow** for applications. This page is a quick orientation; full usage is in [anyhow and thiserror](/rust/anyhow-and-thiserror/).

## The library vs application distinction

This distinction drives which crate to reach for:

- **Writing a library** that others will depend on? Your callers need to be able to `match` on *specific* error variants to handle different failures differently. Use **thiserror** to define a proper enum error type, as shown on the previous page.
- **Writing an application** (a CLI tool, a server, a script) that's the "end of the line" — nothing else depends on it as a library? You usually just want to propagate *any* error upward, log it or print it, and exit. Use **anyhow**, which provides a single `anyhow::Error` type that can wrap *any* error, so you don't need to define a custom enum at all.

## anyhow in practice

```rust
use anyhow::{Context, Result}; // anyhow::Result<T> = Result<T, anyhow::Error>

fn read_config() -> Result<String> {
    let contents = std::fs::read_to_string("config.txt")
        .context("failed to read config.txt")?;
    Ok(contents)
}

fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let config = read_config()?;
    println!("{config}");
    Ok(())
}
```

`.context(...)` attaches a human-readable message to an error as it propagates, without needing a custom error type — when this fails, the printed error chain reads like `"failed to read config.txt: No such file or directory (os error 2)"`, giving you both the high-level explanation and the underlying cause.

## Quick decision guide

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Writing a reusable library (crates.io, or a shared internal crate) | `thiserror` — callers need specific, matchable error variants |
| Writing a CLI tool, server, or script (an application, not a library) | `anyhow` — you just want errors to propagate with good context |
| Small example or learning exercise | Plain `Result<T, String>` or `.unwrap()` is fine — don't reach for a crate until you feel the pain of not having one |

Both crates are covered with full setup instructions in [anyhow and thiserror](/rust/anyhow-and-thiserror/), in the Popular Crates section.

Modules and Crates.Packages, Crates and Modules:
Rust has a specific vocabulary for how code is organized at different scales, and it's worth being precise about each term since they're easy to conflate as a beginner.

## Package

A **package** is what `cargo new` creates — a directory with a `Cargo.toml` file describing it. A package can contain one library crate and/or multiple binary crates, but at most one library.

## Crate

A **crate** is the smallest unit the compiler treats as one compilation unit — either a **binary crate** (compiles to an executable, has a `fn main()`) or a **library crate** (compiles to something other crates can depend on, no `main`). When you write `cargo add rand`, "rand" is the name of a crate (hosted on crates.io). A single package's `src/main.rs` is the root of its binary crate; `src/lib.rs` is the root of its library crate.

```
my_package/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── main.rs   # root of the binary crate (if present)
    └── lib.rs    # root of the library crate (if present)
```

A package with both `main.rs` and `lib.rs` is common: the library crate holds the real logic, and the binary crate is a thin wrapper that calls into it — this makes the logic testable and reusable independent of the CLI/binary layer.

## Module

A **module** (declared with the `mod` keyword) is how you organize code *within* a crate — grouping related functions, structs, and other items, and controlling what's public vs private. Modules are covered in depth on the next two pages: [The Module Tree and Paths](/rust/the-module-tree-and-paths/) and [Separating Modules Into Files](/rust/separating-modules-into-files/).

## The hierarchy, visually

```
Package (Cargo.toml + src/)
 └── Crate (main.rs or lib.rs, and everything it pulls in)
      └── Modules (mod some_module { ... }, organizing code within the crate)
           └── Items (functions, structs, enums, traits, constants...)
```

## Where dependencies fit in

When your `Cargo.toml` lists `serde = "1.0"`, you're depending on the **serde** package, and specifically pulling in its **library crate**. This is why you sometimes see the distinction matter: a package on crates.io can only publish one library crate (what you `use` in your code) but can also ship multiple binary crates (extra command-line tools bundled with it) — `cargo`'s own package, for instance, ships several binaries.

Next: [The Module Tree and Paths](/rust/the-module-tree-and-paths/).
Modules and Crates.Separating Modules Into Files:
Defining every module inline in one file (as on the previous page) doesn't scale. This page covers splitting modules across multiple files — the normal way any real Rust project is organized.

## The basic pattern

Given this module declaration in `src/lib.rs`:

```rust
mod front_of_house;
```

Note: no curly-brace body, just a semicolon. This tells Rust: *"the `front_of_house` module's contents live in another file — go find it."* Rust looks for the module's content in one of two places:

- `src/front_of_house.rs`, or
- `src/front_of_house/mod.rs` (the older style, still valid, less common in new code)

```rust
// src/front_of_house.rs
pub mod hosting; // this submodule's content is in yet another file
```

```rust
// src/front_of_house/hosting.rs
pub fn add_to_waitlist() {}
```

Notice the nesting: because `hosting` is declared *inside* `front_of_house.rs`, its own file lives inside a folder named after the parent module: `src/front_of_house/hosting.rs`.

## A typical multi-file project layout

```
src/
├── main.rs          # mod cli; mod config; ...
├── cli.rs
├── config.rs
└── models/
    ├── mod.rs        # or models.rs, depending on style — pub mod user; pub mod order;
    ├── user.rs
    └── order.rs
```

## The two valid styles for a module with submodules

Both of these are valid and you'll see both in real projects:

```
src/
├── models.rs          # STYLE A (newer, more common): sibling file + folder
└── models/
    ├── user.rs
    └── order.rs
```

```
src/
└── models/
    ├── mod.rs          # STYLE B (older): mod.rs inside the folder itself
    ├── user.rs
    └── order.rs
```

Style A (a `.rs` file alongside a same-named folder) is generally preferred in modern Rust, mainly because having many files all named `mod.rs` open in an editor's tabs is confusing — a` models.rs` tab is immediately identifiable, while a `mod.rs` tab isn't, without also checking which folder it's in.

## Rule of thumb for when to split

As a beginner working through small examples, a single `main.rs` is completely fine. Split into modules/files once a file grows large enough that scrolling to find things becomes annoying — there's no hard rule, but many Rust developers start reaching for separate files somewhere around a few hundred lines in one file, or as soon as there's a natural, clearly separable concept (like "all the HTTP route handlers" or "all the database models") worth its own file.

Modules and Crates.Workspaces:
A **workspace** lets you manage several related packages together — sharing one `Cargo.lock` file and one `target/` build directory, so they compile against consistent dependency versions and don't duplicate build artifacts.

## When you'd want a workspace

- A project with a library crate **and** a separate CLI binary crate that depends on it.
- A larger application split into several internal crates for compile-time and organizational reasons (a `core` crate, an `api` crate, a `cli` crate).
- Several genuinely separate but related tools that should be developed and versioned together.

## Setting one up

```
my_workspace/
├── Cargo.toml       # the workspace root — no [package], just [workspace]
├── core/
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src/lib.rs
└── cli/
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/main.rs
```

```toml
# my_workspace/Cargo.toml
[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = [
    "core",
    "cli",
]
```

```toml
# my_workspace/cli/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "cli"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
core = { path = "../core" } # depend on the sibling crate by relative path
```

## Working with a workspace

From the workspace root, most Cargo commands operate across every member by default:

```bash
cargo build             # builds every member
cargo test               # tests every member
cargo build -p cli        # build just the `cli` package
cargo run -p cli           # run just the `cli` package's binary
```

A single `Cargo.lock` at the workspace root is shared by all members, guaranteeing they all build against the exact same dependency versions — this avoids the situation where two crates in the same project accidentally end up depending on two different, possibly incompatible, versions of some shared dependency.

## When you don't need a workspace

For a single application or library — the overwhelming majority of learning projects and even many real-world ones — a plain `cargo new` package is all you need. Reach for a workspace once you find yourself wanting to split code into genuinely separate, independently-versionable crates, not before.

Generics and Traits.Common Derivable Traits:
You've seen `#[derive(...)]` throughout this guide already. This page consolidates the traits you'll derive constantly, so you know exactly what each one gives you.

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

`#[derive(...)]` generates a trait implementation automatically, based purely on the type's structure (for a struct: derive it for every field; for an enum: derive it for every variant's data) — it saves you from writing boilerplate that would otherwise be entirely mechanical.

## Debug

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
println!("{p:?}");  // Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
println!("{p:#?}"); // pretty-printed, multi-line version
```

Enables the `{:?}` formatting specifier — used constantly for debugging/printing values that don't have a "nice" human-readable `Display` format. Nearly every struct and enum you write should derive `Debug`; there's very little downside.

## Clone and Copy

Covered in full in [Clone and Copy](/rust/clone-and-copy/) — `Clone` adds an explicit `.clone()` method; `Copy` (only derivable if every field is itself `Copy`) makes the type implicitly duplicate on assignment instead of moving.

## PartialEq and Eq

```rust
#[derive(PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

let a = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
let b = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
println!("{}", a == b); // true
```

`PartialEq` enables `==`/`!=`. `Eq` is a marker trait (no methods) indicating equality is *total* (reflexive: every value equals itself) — required by some collections like `HashMap` keys. Floats derive `PartialEq` but not `Eq`, because `NaN != NaN`, which violates `Eq`'s requirement.

## PartialOrd and Ord

```rust
#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Version { major: u32, minor: u32 }
```

Enables `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, and — importantly — `.sort()` on a `Vec` of the type. Derived ordering compares fields **in declaration order**: `major` first, then `minor` only if `major` is equal — this field order matters and is a common source of "why did my sort come out wrong" bugs if fields are declared in an order that doesn't match the intended sort priority.

## Default

```rust
#[derive(Default)]
struct Config {
    verbose: bool,     // defaults to false
    retries: u32,       // defaults to 0
    name: String,        // defaults to ""
}

let config = Config::default();
let custom = Config { verbose: true, ..Default::default() }; // override just one field
```

Generates a `::default()` associated function that builds an instance using each field type's own default. Extremely useful combined with struct update syntax (`..Default::default()`) for config-style structs where callers usually only want to override a couple of fields.

## Hash

```rust
#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
struct UserId(u64);

use std::collections::HashSet;
let mut seen: HashSet<UserId> = HashSet::new();
```

Required for a type to be used as a `HashMap`/`HashSet` key — covered in [HashMap and HashSet](/rust/hashmap-and-hashset/). Note `Hash` is typically derived alongside `Eq`, since the two need to agree (equal values must hash equally).

Strings and Text.String vs str:
Rust has two main string types, and understanding the difference is one of the more genuinely confusing parts of learning Rust — this page aims to make it click permanently.

## String: owned, growable, heap-allocated

```rust
let mut s = String::new();
let s = String::from("hello");
let s = "hello".to_string();
let s = "hello".to_owned();

let mut s = String::from("hello");
s.push_str(", world"); // append a &str
s.push('!');            // append a single char
```

A `String` owns its data on the heap — it's the type you use when you're **building or modifying** text, or when a struct needs to **own** its text data rather than borrow it.

## &str: a borrowed string slice

```rust
let s: &str = "hello"; // string literal — this is ALWAYS a &str, baked into the binary
let s2: &str = &some_string[..]; // a slice/view into a String's data
```

`&str` ("string slice," pronounced "ampersand-str" or "string ref") is a *reference* to string data — either to a literal baked into your compiled binary (which has `'static` lifetime, existing for the whole program), or to a portion of a `String`'s heap data. `&str` never owns anything; it's always borrowing from somewhere.

## Why function parameters should almost always be &str

```rust
fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

fn main() {
    let owned = String::from("Ferris");
    let literal = "World";

    println!("{}", greet(&owned));   // &String auto-coerces to &str
    println!("{}", greet(literal)); // literal is already &str
}
```

`&str` is strictly more flexible as a parameter type: it accepts both string literals *and* references to `String`s (via automatic deref coercion), while a `&String` parameter only accepts the latter. This is exactly the same principle as `&[T]` vs `&Vec<T>` from [Slices](/rust/slices/) — prefer the borrowed slice type in function signatures, and reserve the owning type (`String`, `Vec<T>`) for when you actually need to own or store the data (e.g. a struct field, or a value you're building up).

## The conversion cheat sheet

```rust
let s: String = String::from("hello");   // &str literal -> String
let s: String = "hello".to_string();       // same, different spelling
let s: String = "hello".to_owned();         // same, general-purpose trait method
let s: String = format!("{} {}", "a", "b"); // build via formatting

let slice: &str = &s;          // String -> &str (borrow, via deref coercion)
let slice: &str = s.as_str();   // same, explicit
```

## Why Rust has two string types at all

This isn't complexity for its own sake — it's the same ownership/borrowing distinction from [Ownership and Memory](/rust/why-ownership-exists/), applied to text specifically: `String` is the owned, heap-allocated version (like `Vec<u8>`, roughly); `&str` is the borrowed view (like `&[u8]`, roughly). Once you're comfortable with ownership generally, `String`/`&str` stops feeling like a special case and becomes just one more instance of a pattern you already know.

Strings and Text.String Formatting:
Rust's formatting system, used by `println!`, `format!`, `write!`, and friends, is one of the more powerful and pleasant corners of the language.

## The basics

```rust
let name = "Ferris";
let age = 8;

println!("Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old."); // captured identifiers (modern, preferred)
println!("Hello, {}! You are {} years old.", name, age); // positional (older style, still common)
println!("{0} is {1}. {0} likes Rust.", name, "great");   // indexed, for reuse
```

Since Rust 2021, you can interpolate variables **directly inside the braces** (`{name}`) as long as the variable is already in scope — this is now the preferred, idiomatic style for simple cases.

## format!, print!, println!, eprintln!

```rust
let s: String = format!("{} and {}", "salt", "pepper"); // builds a String, doesn't print
print!("no newline");
println!("with a newline");
eprintln!("goes to stderr, not stdout"); // for error/diagnostic output
```

## Debug vs Display formatting

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };

println!("{p:?}");  // Debug: Point { x: 1, y: 2 } — requires #[derive(Debug)]
println!("{p:#?}"); // pretty Debug, multi-line
```

`{}` (Display) requires implementing `std::fmt::Display` yourself (there's no derive for it, because a "nice" human-readable format is inherently type-specific and can't be inferred structurally):

```rust
use std::fmt;

impl fmt::Display for Point {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "({}, {})", self.x, self.y)
    }
}

println!("{p}"); // (1, 2) — now works, via Display
```

## Number formatting

```rust
let pi = 3.14159265;

println!("{pi:.2}");     // 3.14 — 2 decimal places
println!("{pi:10.2}");   // "      3.14" — width 10, right-aligned, 2 decimals
println!("{pi:<10.2}");  // "3.14      " — left-aligned
println!("{pi:^10.2}");  // "   3.14   " — center-aligned

let n = 42;
println!("{n:5}");   // "   42" — width 5, right-aligned (default for numbers)
println!("{n:05}");  // "00042" — zero-padded
println!("{n:x}");   // "2a" — hexadecimal
println!("{n:#x}");  // "0x2a" — hex with 0x prefix
println!("{n:b}");   // "101010" — binary
println!("{n:o}");   // "52" — octal
```

## Debugging quickly with dbg!

```rust
let x = 5;
let y = dbg!(x * 2); // prints "[src/main.rs:2:13] x * 2 = 10" to stderr,
                       // AND returns the value, so it can be inlined anywhere
```

`dbg!` is genuinely useful for quick "what is this value right now" debugging — unlike `println!`, it also prints the file, line number, and the expression's source text, and it returns the value so you can wrap it around any expression without restructuring your code.

Strings and Text.Working With Text:
This page covers common string operations and the UTF-8-related gotchas that trip up newcomers.

## Common string methods

```rust
let s = "  Hello, World!  ";

s.trim();                 // "Hello, World!" — removes leading/trailing whitespace
s.to_uppercase();          // "  HELLO, WORLD!  "
s.to_lowercase();           // "  hello, world!  "
s.len();                     // byte length, NOT necessarily character count (see below)
s.is_empty();                 // false
s.contains("World");           // true
s.starts_with("  Hello");       // true
s.ends_with("!  ");              // true
s.replace("World", "Rust");       // "  Hello, Rust!  "
s.split(",").collect::<Vec<_>>(); // ["  Hello", " World!  "]
s.split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<_>>(); // ["Hello,", "World!"]
```

## Splitting and parsing

```rust
let csv_line = "Alice,30,Engineer";
let fields: Vec<&str> = csv_line.split(',').collect();
println!("{fields:?}"); // ["Alice", "30", "Engineer"]

let age: i32 = fields[1].parse().expect("not a valid number");
println!("{age}"); // 30
```

`.parse::<T>()` converts a `&str` into any type that implements `FromStr` (most built-in numeric types, `bool`, and many custom types) — it returns a `Result`, since the string might not actually be valid for the target type, so parsing is a great example of where `?` (from [The Question Mark Operator](/rust/the-question-mark-operator/)) is commonly used:

```rust
fn parse_age(input: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    let age: i32 = input.trim().parse()?;
    Ok(age)
}
```

## Why .len() isn't "number of characters"

This is one of the most important gotchas to understand early. Rust `String`s and `&str` are **always valid UTF-8**, and `.len()` returns the number of **bytes**, not the number of visible characters (Unicode "scalar values" or, further still, human-perceived "graphemes"):

```rust
let s = "héllo"; // é is 2 bytes in UTF-8, everything else is 1 byte each
println!("{}", s.len());              // 6, not 5!
println!("{}", s.chars().count());     // 5 — iterate as chars to count "characters"
```

Because of this, **you cannot index a `String` with `s[0]`** the way you might in Python or JavaScript — Rust disallows it entirely, precisely because "the 0th byte" and "the 0th character" are different concepts that would silently produce wrong or even invalid results for non-ASCII text.

```rust
let s = String::from("héllo");
// let c = s[0]; // ERROR: String cannot be indexed by integer — this is intentional!

let first_char = s.chars().next(); // Option<char> -> Some('h') — the correct way
```

## Iterating text correctly

```rust
let s = "héllo";

for c in s.chars() {       // iterate by Unicode scalar value ("character")
    print!("{c} ");
}

for b in s.bytes() {        // iterate by raw byte (rarely what you want for text)
    print!("{b} ");
}
```

For almost all text-processing purposes, `.chars()` is what you want. Slicing a string by byte range (`&s[0..3]`) is still possible and useful when you *do* know you're working with byte offsets (e.g. from `.find()`), but **panics at runtime** if the range doesn't fall on a valid character boundary — so be cautious slicing text that might contain multi-byte characters.

Testing.Organizing Tests:
Rust distinguishes between two kinds of tests, which serve different purposes and live in different places.

## Unit tests: alongside the code, in the same file

As shown on the previous page — a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }` block inside the same file as the code it's testing. Because they're in the same module, unit tests can access **private** functions and items too, not just the public API — this is the main reason they live inline rather than in a separate file.

```rust
// src/lib.rs
fn internal_helper(x: i32) -> i32 { // private — not pub!
    x * 2
}

pub fn public_api(x: i32) -> i32 {
    internal_helper(x) + 1
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn test_internal_helper() {
        assert_eq!(internal_helper(5), 10); // can test private functions directly
    }
}
```

## Integration tests: in a separate tests/ directory

```
my_project/
├── src/
│   └── lib.rs
└── tests/
    ├── basic_integration.rs
    └── another_test_file.rs
```

Each file in `tests/` is compiled as its own separate crate, and can **only** access your crate's `pub` API — exactly as an external user of your library would. This makes integration tests a genuine end-to-end check that your public interface behaves correctly, as opposed to unit tests, which check internal logic.

```rust
// tests/basic_integration.rs
use my_project::public_api; // must go through the public API

#[test]
fn test_public_api() {
    assert_eq!(public_api(5), 11);
}
```

Note: integration tests only apply to **library** crates (with a `src/lib.rs`) — a pure binary crate (`src/main.rs` only, no `lib.rs`) can't be tested this way, since there's no library interface for the `tests/` files to `use`. This is one more reason many real projects split logic into a `lib.rs` even when they also have a `main.rs` — see [Packages, Crates and Modules](/rust/packages-crates-and-modules/).

## Running specific tests

```bash
cargo test                       # run everything
cargo test it_adds                # run only tests whose name contains "it_adds"
cargo test --test basic_integration  # run only one integration test file
cargo test -- --nocapture          # show println! output even for passing tests
cargo test -- --test-threads=1       # run tests sequentially instead of in parallel
```

By default, `cargo test` runs tests in **parallel**, on separate threads — this is fast, but means tests must not depend on shared mutable state (like the same file on disk) unless carefully synchronized, since they may run in any order or at the same time.

## Ignoring slow tests by default

```rust
#[test]
#[ignore] // skipped by default
fn expensive_test() {
    // something that takes a long time
}
```

```bash
cargo test                # skips expensive_test
cargo test -- --ignored    # runs ONLY ignored tests
```

Cargo and Toolchain.Cargo.toml Explained:
`Cargo.toml` is your project's manifest — every setting about the package, its dependencies, and how it should build lives here, in TOML format (a simple, readable configuration language).

## The full anatomy

```toml
[package]
name = "my_project"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
authors = ["Your Name <you@example.com>"]
description = "A short description of what this does."
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"
repository = "https://github.com/you/my_project"
readme = "README.md"
keywords = ["cli", "example"]
categories = ["command-line-utilities"]

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
rand = "0.8"
local_crate = { path = "../local_crate" }
some_git_crate = { git = "https://github.com/someone/some_git_crate" }

[dev-dependencies]
criterion = "0.5" # only used for tests/benchmarks, not the final build

[build-dependencies]
cc = "1.0" # only used by a build.rs script, not the final build

[features]
default = ["std"]
std = []
extra = ["dep:some_optional_crate"]

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = true
panic = "abort"

[[bin]]
name = "my_project"
path = "src/main.rs"
```

## [package]: identity and metadata

`name`, `version`, and `edition` are the only fields `cargo new` fills in by default; the rest matter mainly once you're publishing to crates.io (covered in [Publishing to crates.io](/rust/publishing-to-crates-io/)) — `description`, `license`, and `repository` are effectively required for publishing.

## [dependencies], [dev-dependencies], [build-dependencies]

- **`[dependencies]`** — needed to actually build and run your code.
- **`[dev-dependencies]`** — only needed for `cargo test`, `cargo bench`, or examples; not compiled into your final release binary or included when someone depends on your library.
- **`[build-dependencies]`** — only used by a `build.rs` build script, if you have one (an advanced feature for code generation or linking to native C libraries, not needed for most projects).

## Dependency specification shapes

```toml
[dependencies]
simple = "1.0"                                   # from crates.io, by version
detailed = { version = "1.0", features = ["x"] }   # with specific feature flags
no_default = { version = "1.0", default-features = false } # opt out of default features
local = { path = "../local_crate" }                 # from a local directory
from_git = { git = "https://github.com/user/repo" }  # from a git repository
```

## [features]: optional, opt-in functionality

Features let a crate expose optional functionality that users can enable only if they need it, keeping compile times and binary size down for users who don't. `default = [...]` lists which features are on unless a user opts out with `default-features = false`.

## [profile.release] and [profile.dev]

Controls compiler optimization settings per build mode — covered fully in [Debug vs Release Builds](/rust/debug-vs-release-builds/).

Next: [Dependencies and Semantic Versioning](/rust/dependencies-and-semantic-versioning/).
Cargo and Toolchain.Dependencies and Semantic Versioning:
## Semantic versioning (semver), briefly

Rust's ecosystem relies heavily on **semantic versioning**: a version number `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (e.g. `1.4.2`) where, by convention:

- **MAJOR** increments for breaking changes.
- **MINOR** increments for new, backward-compatible functionality.
- **PATCH** increments for backward-compatible bug fixes.

## How version requirements in Cargo.toml actually work

This is a common point of confusion: `rand = "0.8"` does **not** mean "exactly version 0.8" — it's shorthand for a **caret requirement**, meaning "any version compatible with 0.8, allowing minor and patch updates, but not a breaking major version change":

```toml
rand = "0.8"       # equivalent to: ^0.8, allows 0.8.x and 0.9.x, up to (not including) 1.0.0
rand = "1.2.3"      # ^1.2.3, allows 1.2.3 up to (not including) 2.0.0
rand = "=1.2.3"      # exact version only, no flexibility
rand = "~1.2"          # allows patch updates only: 1.2.x, not 1.3.0
rand = ">=1.2, <1.5"     # explicit range
```

For versions starting with `0.`, caret requirements are stricter: `^0.8` only allows `0.8.x` (patch updates), *not* `0.9.x`, because in semver's convention, a `0.x` major version is considered still unstable, and minor bumps there are allowed to be breaking.

## Cargo.lock: pinning exact versions

`Cargo.toml` specifies acceptable *ranges*; `Cargo.lock` records the **exact** versions that were actually resolved and used for a given build — including every transitive dependency, several layers deep.

- **For binary projects (applications)**: commit `Cargo.lock` to version control. This guarantees everyone on the team, and your CI/CD pipeline, builds with the exact same dependency versions, avoiding "works on my machine" bugs caused by a dependency silently updating.
- **For library projects**: it's common (though not universal) to *not* commit `Cargo.lock` (`cargo new --lib` still generates one, but many library maintainers add it to `.gitignore`), since a library's actual dependency versions should be resolved by whatever application ultimately depends on it, not fixed by the library itself.

## Updating dependencies

```bash
cargo update              # update all dependencies to the latest version allowed by Cargo.toml
cargo update -p rand        # update just one dependency
cargo outdated               # (requires cargo-outdated, installed separately) shows what's available beyond your current ranges
```

`cargo update` respects the ranges in `Cargo.toml` — it won't jump from `0.8` to `1.0` on its own, since that's outside what `rand = "0.8"` permits. To actually take a new major version, you edit `Cargo.toml` yourself (or run `cargo add rand@1.0` again, which updates the requirement explicitly).

## Auditing for security issues

```bash
cargo install cargo-audit
cargo audit
```

`cargo-audit` checks your `Cargo.lock` against the RustSec security advisory database, flagging any dependencies with known vulnerabilities — a good habit to run periodically, or as part of CI, on any real project.

Cargo and Toolchain.rustup, Toolchains and Editions:
This page consolidates and expands on [The Rust Toolchain Explained](/rust/the-rust-toolchain-explained/) from the Getting Started section, now that you have more context for why these concepts matter in practice.

## Listing and managing installed toolchains

```bash
rustup show                     # summary of installed toolchains and the active one
rustup toolchain list              # list installed toolchains
rustup toolchain install nightly     # install an additional toolchain
rustup toolchain uninstall nightly     # remove one
rustup default stable                    # set the global default
rustup update                              # update all installed toolchains to their latest version
```

## Per-directory toolchain overrides

You can pin a specific toolchain for one project without changing your global default, in two ways:

**A `rust-toolchain.toml` file** (recommended — checked into version control, so it's automatic for anyone who clones the repo):

```toml
[toolchain]
channel = "1.96.0"
components = ["clippy", "rustfmt"]
```

**A manual override**, not shared with collaborators:

```bash
rustup override set nightly   # only affects the current directory (and subdirectories)
rustup override unset          # remove the override
```

## Cross-compilation targets

By default, rustup only installs the toolchain for your current machine's target (e.g. `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`). To compile for a *different* platform, you need to add that target first:

```bash
rustup target list                       # see all available targets
rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu     # add a target for cross-compiling to Windows
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown      # add WebAssembly as a target
```

Adding a target alone is often not sufficient for a fully working cross-compile toolchain (you may also need a linker for the target platform) — this is covered in full in [Cross Compiling](/rust/cross-compiling/).

## Editions, revisited: what changed in the 2024 edition

As covered briefly earlier: an edition (`edition = "2024"` in `Cargo.toml`, the current default as of this guide) is a bundle of small, deliberately opt-in syntax and semantics changes, not a new version of the compiler. All editions are supported by the same, current `rustc`, and crates on different editions can freely depend on each other. **The 2024 edition became the default for `cargo new` starting with Rust 1.85** (released February 2025); if you're reading an older tutorial or an existing project that still says `edition = "2021"`, that's not wrong or broken — it simply predates the switch, and 2021-edition code continues to compile correctly under current `rustc` indefinitely.

The 2024 edition's most notable changes, in brief:

- **`unsafe extern` blocks are now required.** An `extern "C" { ... }` block declaring foreign (C) functions must now be written as `unsafe extern "C" { ... }`, making explicit that declaring an external function signature is itself something the compiler can't verify — this mostly affects FFI-heavy code, not typical application code.
- **Tightened `unsafe` attribute requirements.** Certain attributes that have safety implications (like `#[no_mangle]`) must now be written as `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`, for the same "make unsafety visible" reasoning as above.
- **Changes to closure and `impl Trait` capture rules.** Closures and return-position `impl Trait` (covered in [Trait Objects and dyn](/rust/trait-objects-and-dyn/)) now capture only the *specific fields* they actually use from a struct, rather than the whole struct, in more cases — this is a refinement that makes more borrow-checker patterns compile successfully than before, rather than a breaking change you need to react to.
- **`if let` temporary scoping changed.** Temporary values created in an `if let` condition's scrutinee now drop at the end of the `if let` block rather than lingering — this occasionally changes the exact moment a `Drop` implementation runs, relevant mainly if you rely on `Drop` side effects (like a `MutexGuard` releasing a lock) at a precise point.
- **`gen` is now a reserved keyword**, reserved for an upcoming generator-function feature — existing code using `gen` as an identifier needs renaming, though this is rare in practice.

None of this changes anything taught in the earlier sections of this guide — ownership, borrowing, structs, traits, error handling, and the standard library all behave identically across the 2021 and 2024 editions at the level covered here. The differences matter mainly for `unsafe`/FFI code and some advanced trait/closure edge cases.

## Checking what's installed, quickly

```bash
rustc --version --verbose
```

This single command is often the fastest way to confirm exactly what toolchain, host platform, and LLVM version you're building with — genuinely useful when debugging a "works on one machine, not another" issue.

Cargo and Toolchain.clippy and rustfmt:
Two official tools round out the daily Rust workflow: **clippy**, a linter that catches common mistakes and suggests more idiomatic code, and **rustfmt**, the code formatter. Both are installed by default with a standard rustup install.

## clippy

```bash
cargo clippy
```

Clippy catches things the compiler itself doesn't consider *errors*, but that are almost always mistakes or suboptimal style — for example:

```rust
// clippy warns: "using `clone` on a `Copy` type"
let x: i32 = 5;
let y = x.clone(); // unnecessary — i32 is Copy, just do `let y = x;`

// clippy warns: "this `if` has identical blocks"
if condition {
    do_something();
} else {
    do_something();
}

// clippy warns: "needless return statement"
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    return a + b; // just `a + b` without `return` is idiomatic here
}
```

Clippy's lints are grouped into categories, some on by default, some opt-in:

```bash
cargo clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic   # enable a stricter, opt-in lint group
cargo clippy -- -D warnings             # treat all warnings as errors (common in CI)
```

Silencing a specific lint, when you've deliberately decided against its suggestion:

```rust
#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]
fn many_args(a: i32, b: i32, c: i32, d: i32, e: i32, f: i32, g: i32, h: i32) {}
```

## rustfmt

```bash
cargo fmt              # format the whole project in place
cargo fmt -- --check     # check only — exit non-zero if anything WOULD be reformatted (for CI)
```

Rustfmt's defaults are the community-standard style — virtually no Rust project deviates from them significantly, which means Rust code from wildly different authors and projects tends to look remarkably consistent.

## Customizing rustfmt (rarely needed)

A `rustfmt.toml` (or `.rustfmt.toml`) file at your project root can tweak a limited set of settings:

```toml
max_width = 100
tab_spaces = 4
edition = "2024"
```

Most projects don't customize this at all — leaning on the defaults is the norm and generally recommended, since it keeps formatting consistent with the rest of the ecosystem.

## Wiring both into your editor

With rust-analyzer configured (see [Your Editor Setup](/rust/your-editor-setup/)), format-on-save runs `rustfmt` automatically, and clippy warnings/errors appear inline as you type, alongside regular compiler diagnostics — set this up once and you'll rarely need to invoke either command manually.

## A common CI check

```bash
cargo fmt -- --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo test
```

This three-command sequence — formatting is correct, no clippy warnings, and all tests pass — is a very common baseline for a Rust project's continuous integration pipeline.

Building and Shipping.Debug vs Release Builds:
## The two default build profiles

```bash
cargo build           # debug profile — fast to compile, unoptimized, includes debug symbols
cargo build --release   # release profile — slow to compile, heavily optimized, no debug symbols by default
```

| | Debug (`cargo build`) | Release (`cargo build --release`) |
|---|---|---|
| Output location | `target/debug/` | `target/release/` |
| Compile speed | Fast | Slow (much more optimization work) |
| Runtime speed | Slow (often 10-100x slower for CPU-heavy code) | Fast — this is the whole point |
| Binary size | Larger | Smaller (usually) |
| Overflow checks | Panics on integer overflow | Silently wraps (by default) |
| Debug assertions (`debug_assert!`) | Active | Stripped out entirely |

**Use debug builds while developing** — `cargo run`, `cargo test`, and your editor's rust-analyzer all default to debug mode, prioritizing fast iteration over runtime performance. **Use `--release` for anything you actually ship or benchmark** — a debug build's performance is not representative of what users will experience.

## Customizing profiles in Cargo.toml

```toml
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3       # 0-3, or "s"/"z" for size-optimized; 3 is the default for release
lto = true           # Link-Time Optimization — slower compile, often faster/smaller output
codegen-units = 1      # fewer parallel codegen units = better optimization, slower compile
panic = "abort"          # skip unwinding on panic — smaller, sometimes faster binary
strip = true               # strip debug symbols from the final binary — smaller file size

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1         # a LITTLE optimization even in debug mode — common for perf-sensitive dev work,
                       # e.g. games or number-crunching where fully unoptimized is painfully slow
```

`lto = true` and `codegen-units = 1` are common in performance-critical release builds (increasing compile time noticeably in exchange for a faster or smaller final binary) — for most everyday projects, the release profile's defaults are already good, and these are optimizations worth reaching for only once you're specifically trying to squeeze out more performance or reduce binary size.

## debug_assert! for development-only checks

```rust
fn calculate(x: i32) -> i32 {
    debug_assert!(x >= 0, "x should never be negative here");
    x * 2
}
```

`debug_assert!` behaves like `assert!` in debug builds, but is compiled out entirely (zero runtime cost) in release builds — useful for sanity-checking internal invariants during development without paying any cost in the shipped binary.

## Measuring binary size

```bash
cargo build --release
ls -lh target/release/my_app     # Linux/macOS
```

If binary size matters (embedded targets, distributing many copies, WebAssembly), the combination of `strip = true`, `opt-level = "z"`, `lto = true`, and `panic = "abort"` in `[profile.release]` can meaningfully shrink output — often by 30-70% compared to unconfigured defaults, though the exact impact varies a lot by project.
